sql_schemas: table leave_requests | fields: id, employee_id, leave_type_code, start_date, end_date, requested_days, reason, status, approver_id, approval_comment, submitted_at, decided_at, cancelled_by, cancelled_at, reverses_request_id | pk: id | fks: employee_id -> employees.id; leave_type_code -> leave_types.code; approver_id -> employees.id; cancelled_by -> employees.id; reverses_request_id -> leave_requests.id | indexes: id: primary key; every findById / update / route :id lookup resolves on it; reverses_request_id: UNIQUE (nullable) — the database-level backstop for 'release the balance exactly once': at most one reversal row may reference a given original, so a concurrent or repeated cancel of the same APPROVED request cannot insert a second reversal and double-release usedDays. The same index serves the findByReversesRequestId lookup the service uses to detect an existing reversal before writing. Nullable because the overwhelming majority of rows (every non-reversal request) carry no value; a unique index tolerates multiple NULLs.; employee_id, status: existing composite index — role-scoped list queries (EMPLOYEE -> own id, MANAGER -> self + direct reports) filter on employee_id and frequently on status; also serves the owner/status guards on submit/approve/reject/cancel; leave_type_code, start_date: existing index — supports the leaveTypeCode filter and the inclusive startDateFrom/startDateTo range filters in findByQuery, and the ORDER BY start_date DESC list ordering; status: status-filtered list queries and the 'is there already a CANCELLED reversal for this original' scan; employee_id: FK lookups and per-employee history reads

table leave_balances | fields: id, employee_id, leave_type_code, period_start, period_end, entitled_days, used_days, pending_days | pk: id | fks: employee_id -> employees.id; leave_type_code -> leave_types.code | indexes: id: primary key; the update target for the balance release; employee_id, leave_type_code, period_start, period_end: UNIQUE — findByKey resolves exactly one balance row per employee/type/period; the release path reads it with a row lock (forUpdate) before writing used_days, so this index is also the lock target; employee_id: per-employee balance reads (GET /balances/me)

table audit_logs | fields: id, actor_id, action, entity_type, entity_id, before_state, after_state, occurred_at | pk: id | fks: actor_id -> employees.id | indexes: id: primary key; findById lookup; entity_type, entity_id: the audit trail for one leave request is read by entity, and the reversal writes a CANCEL entry against the ORIGINAL request id (entityId = original id) so the trail stays attached to the approved row; actor_id: 'what did this actor do' queries

table notifications | fields: id, recipient_id, type, title, message, related_entity_type, related_entity_id, status, created_at, read_at | pk: id | fks: recipient_id -> employees.id | indexes: id: primary key; findById lookup; recipient_id, status: the inbox read pattern (unread notifications for one recipient); related_entity_type, related_entity_id: the cancellation notification points at the ORIGINAL request id, so the notification is discoverable from the approved row

methods: create(input: CreateLeaveRequestInput, client?: PoolClient): Promise<LeaveRequest> — inserts all 15 columns including reverses_request_id; used for the NEW CANCELLED reversal row
findById(id: string, client?: PoolClient): Promise<LeaveRequest | null> — returns null when absent; the service decides error semantics

findByReversesRequestId(reversesRequestId: string, client?: PoolClient): Promise<LeaveRequest | null> — NEW; resolves the reversal row for an original id so the service can detect an already-reversed APPROVED request before releasing the balance a second time

update(id: string, changes: UpdateLeaveRequestDto, client?: PoolClient): Promise<LeaveRequest> — dynamic SET from FIELD_COLUMNS; used ONLY for the in-place DRAFT/SUBMITTED cancellation (status/cancelledBy/cancelledAt). MUST NOT be called with the id of an APPROVED row (GP-008)

findByQuery(params: LeaveRequestQueryParams, client?: PoolClient): Promise<LeaveRequest[]> — status/leaveTypeCode/date-range/employeeIds filters plus limit/offset, ORDER BY start_date DESC; returns both the original APPROVED row and its CANCELLED reversal row, each carrying reverses_request_id so the client can tell them apart
repositories.backing: PostgreSQL via the shared pg Pool (src/shared/db/connection.ts, constructor-injected `dbPool` defaulting to `defaultPool`); every method takes an optional trailing `PoolClient` and falls back to the shared pool when omitted — the repository never opens BEGIN/COMMIT/ROLLBACK

methods: findByKey(employeeId, leaveTypeCode, periodStart, periodEnd, client?, forUpdate?): Promise<LeaveBalance | null> — the release path passes forUpdate=true so the row is locked before the used_days delta is computed in application code

update(id: string, changes: { entitledDays?, usedDays?, pendingDays? }, client?: PoolClient): Promise<LeaveBalance> — the single write that releases requestedDays back to usedDays (APPROVED cancellation) or decrements pendingDays (SUBMITTED cancellation); throws NotFoundError on a missing row
findById(id: string, client?: PoolClient): Promise<LeaveBalance | null>
repositories.backing: PostgreSQL via the shared pg Pool (src/shared/db/connection.ts); optional trailing `PoolClient` on every method so the release joins the caller's transaction

methods: create(input: CreateAuditLogInput, client?: PoolClient): Promise<AuditLog> — generates id via randomUUID(), stamps occurredAt, JSON-stringifies before_state/after_state; the reversal writes action CANCEL with entityId = the ORIGINAL request id and beforeState = the untouched APPROVED row
findById(id: string, client?: PoolClient): Promise<AuditLog | null>
repositories.backing: PostgreSQL via the shared pg Pool (src/shared/db/connection.ts); optional trailing `PoolClient` so the CANCEL audit entry joins the caller's transaction

methods: create(input: CreateNotificationInput, client?: PoolClient): Promise<Notification> — generates id/createdAt, defaults status to PENDING; relatedEntityId = the ORIGINAL request id
findById(id: string, client?: PoolClient): Promise<Notification | null>

data_notes:
Persistence slice for GP-008 reversal. One schema change: a new nullable `reverses_request_id` column on `leave_requests` (FK -> leave_requests.id, UNIQUE) plus a knex migration; no other table changes. `leave_requests` is defined exactly once here and referenced by name by every repository that touches it.

Key design points:
- The APPROVED row is never written. `PgLeaveRequestRepository.update` is used only for the in-place DRAFT/SUBMITTED cancellation; the APPROVED path inserts a NEW row via `create` with status CANCELLED and reverses_request_id = original id. The original's status/approver_id/approval_comment/decided_at are untouched by construction.
- The UNIQUE index on reverses_request_id is the database-level backstop for "release exactly once": at most one reversal row can reference a given original, so a concurrent or repeated cancel cannot insert a second reversal and double-release used_days. The service additionally checks `findByReversesRequestId` inside the transaction before writing.
- Balance release is unchanged in amount and direction: APPROVED -> used_days -= requestedDays; SUBMITTED -> pending_days -= requestedDays; DRAFT -> no balance read or write. The balance row is read with forUpdate=true before the write, exactly as submit/approve/reject.
- The CANCEL audit entry and the cancellation notification both point at the ORIGINAL request id (entityId / relatedEntityId), so the immutable approved row keeps its full trail; the reversal row is discoverable from it via reverses_request_id.
- Read model: `findByQuery` returns both rows; `reverses_request_id` is exposed on the LeaveRequest model so GET /leaves lets a client tell the original APPROVED row from its CANCELLED reversal. No new endpoint, no new repository interface — `ILeaveRepository` gains one method (`findByReversesRequestId`).

Two genuinely undecided semantics are recorded as openQuestions rather than silently asserted: (1) whether the reversal row duplicates requestedDays/dates and which row's day count drives the release; (2) whether the reversal row copies approverId/decidedAt or leaves them null. Both affect double-counting in future aggregations and must be settled before the code agent writes the insert.

open_questions.question: Which row's requestedDays drives the balance release on an APPROVED cancellation, and does the new CANCELLED reversal row duplicate requestedDays/startDate/endDate from the original?
open_questions.impact: The release amount must be returned exactly once and must not be double-counted. If the reversal row copies requestedDays and a future consumer (a report, a balance recomputation, a list aggregation) sums requestedDays over CANCELLED rows, the same days are counted twice — once on the immutable APPROVED original and once on the reversal. The choice also determines whether the reversal row is self-describing (readable without joining back to the original) or a thin pointer.
candidate_options: Reversal row copies requestedDays/startDate/endDate/leaveTypeCode/employeeId from the original; the release reads the ORIGINAL's requestedDays (the reversal row is a self-describing snapshot, and any aggregation must filter on reverses_request_id IS NULL)
Reversal row copies the same fields AND the release reads the REVERSAL row's requestedDays (single source for the release, but the two rows must be kept equal by construction)

Reversal row carries only id/employeeId/leaveTypeCode/status/reversesRequestId/cancelledBy/cancelledAt; the release and every read join back to the original for dates and day count (no duplication, but the reversal row is not independently readable and the list read model must join)

open_questions.question: Should the new CANCELLED reversal row carry the original's approverId/decidedAt (a copy of the completed approval) or leave them null?
open_questions.impact: GP-008 makes the original's approverId/approvalComment/decidedAt immutable, but says nothing about the reversal row. If the reversal row copies them, a reader that filters on approverId or decidedAt (e.g. an approver's decision history, or a 'decided in this period' report) sees the same decision twice — once on the APPROVED original and once on the CANCELLED reversal. If they are null, the reversal row cannot be attributed to the approval that it reverses without a join, and any code that assumes 'decidedAt set implies a decision was made on this row' stays honest.
candidate_options: Reversal row leaves approverId/approvalComment/decidedAt null — the decision lives only on the immutable original, reachable via reversesRequestId
Reversal row copies approverId/decidedAt from the original as a denormalized snapshot of the approval it reverses
Reversal row sets approverId to the actor who performed the reversal and decidedAt to the reversal time (reusing the columns for the reversal decision, which overloads their meaning)

transaction_contract:
Multi-step atomic write — required. Cancelling an APPROVED request performs, in one unit of work: (a) insert the new CANCELLED reversal row, (b) release requestedDays from used_days on the balance row, (c) write the CANCEL audit entry, (d) insert the cancellation notification. A partial commit would either release the balance with no reversal row (days lost, no record) or insert the reversal with no release (days never returned) — both violate "returned exactly once".

Contract: repository and service methods that must join a caller's transaction take an OPTIONAL trailing `client?: PoolClient` parameter, defaulting to the shared pool (`src/shared/db/connection.ts`) when omitted. The calling service owns the unit of work: `LeaveService.cancel` calls `this.uow.withTransaction(async (client) => { ... })` (PgUnitOfWork acquires a client from the shared pool, BEGIN, runs the callback, COMMIT on resolve / ROLLBACK on throw, always releases). Inside the callback the same `client` is threaded to every participating call: `repository.findByReversesRequestId(originalId, client)`, `repository.create(reversalInput, client)`, `balanceRepository.findByKey(..., client, true)` (row lock) then `balanceRepository.update(balanceId, { usedDays: ... }, client)`, `auditService.record(entry, client)`, `notificationService.create(input, client)`. BEGIN/COMMIT/ROLLBACK appear only in PgUnitOfWork — never in a repository or service. The DRAFT/SUBMITTED in-place cancellation uses the same contract (update + balance release + audit + notification in one transaction). Read paths (`list`, `getById`) open no transaction and forward no client.
